nginx-variable-expand.title: Expand NGINX Variables in a String
nginx-variable-expand.description:
Directives such as `return`, `proxy_set_header` and `log_format` accept text with **variables** inside, for example
`https://$host$request_uri`. Write `expand_vars(template, variables)` that returns the text with every variable replaced.

Rules:

- A variable is written `$name` or `${name}`. A name starts with a letter or underscore and continues with letters,
  digits or underscores. `$name` takes the **longest** valid name, so `$hostname` is the variable `hostname`, never
  `host` followed by `name`. Braces mark where the name ends: `${host}name`.
- A variable that is not in `variables` becomes the empty string.
- A `$` that is not followed by a valid name (or by `{name}`) stays in the output unchanged.
- Substitution happens **once**: a `$` inside a substituted value is not expanded again.

**Example:** `"$scheme://$host$request_uri"` with `{"scheme": "https", "host": "shop.test", "request_uri": "/a?b=1"}`
→ `"https://shop.test/a?b=1"`

**Example:** `"${host}name $hostname"` with `{"host": "a", "hostname": "b"}` → `"aname b"`

guide.prereqs: Strings and dictionaries. Lesson: *Installing NGINX and reading nginx.conf* (variables).
guide.intuition: Scan the text once from left to right. Each time you meet `$`, read the longest name that follows, look it up, and write the value. Never look at the output again.
hints: A regular expression with two alternatives handles both spellings: `\$\{name\}` and `\$name`.
`re.sub` accepts a function as the replacement; it is called once per match with the match object.
Use `variables.get(name, "")` so that unknown variables vanish instead of raising an error.
guide.brute_force: Loop over the dictionary and call `str.replace` for each key. It is short and wrong twice over: `$host` also eats the start of `$hostname`, and a value containing `$x` gets expanded again by a later replacement.
guide.approach:
1. Write a pattern for a name: `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*`.
2. Combine `\$\{NAME\}` and `\$NAME` with `|`, capturing the name in each.
3. In the callback take whichever group matched and return `variables.get(name, "")`.

Dry run on `${host}name $hostname` with host=a, hostname=b: the first match is `${host}` → `a`; `name` is copied; the second match is `$hostname` (the regex is greedy) → `b`. Result `aname b`.
guide.complexity: Time O(n) for a template of n characters plus the length of the substituted values; space O(output).
guide.pitfalls: Replacing shorter names first; expanding substituted values again; treating `$5` or a lone `$` as a variable; forgetting the braces form.
guide.follow_up: NGINX also has positional captures `$1`..`$9` from the last regex match. Extend the function to take a list of captures.

nginx-server-block-select.title: Choose the Server Block
nginx-server-block-select.description:
Implement both stages NGINX uses to pick a `server` block.

`select_server(servers, local_ip, port, host)` returns the **index** of the chosen server, or `-1` if no server listens
for that connection. Each server is `[listen, names, is_default]`:

- `listen` is `"IP:PORT"` or `"*:PORT"` (every address).
- `names` is the list from `server_name`.
- `is_default` is `True` when the listen line carries `default_server`.

**Stage A (listen socket).** Candidates are the servers whose `listen` equals `local_ip:port` exactly. Only if there are
none, the candidates are the servers listening on `*:port`.

**Stage B (name).** Lower-case `host` and drop a `:port` suffix. If it is non-empty, test the candidates in this order
and stop at the first rule that produces a match:

1. **Exact name.** A name beginning with a dot, `.example.com`, also counts as the exact name `example.com`.
2. **Longest wildcard at the start**: `*.example.com` (or the dot form `.example.com`) matches any host ending in
   `.example.com` with at least one character before it.
3. **Longest wildcard at the end**: `www.example.*` matches any host starting with `www.example.` with at least one
   character after it.
4. **First regular expression** in configuration order. A regex name starts with `~`; test the rest with `re.search`.

Within a rule, ties go to the earlier server. If nothing matched (or `host` is empty or `None`), choose the candidate
with `is_default`, and if none has it, the **first candidate**.

**Example:** servers `[["*:80", ["_"], True], ["*:80", ["shop.test"], False], ["*:80", ["*.shop.test"], False]]`,
connection to `203.0.113.10` port `80`: host `"www.shop.test"` → `2`; host `"other.example"` → `0`.

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *Serving a first static site and choosing a server block*. String methods `startswith`, `endswith`; `re.search`.
guide.intuition: NGINX narrows twice. First by where the connection arrived (address and port), then by the name the client asked for. Names are tried by kind, most specific kind first; file order only breaks ties inside a kind and orders the regexes.
hints: Build the candidate list first. An address-specific `listen` beats `*:port` completely: if any exist, wildcard listeners are not candidates at all.
Do four separate passes over the candidates (exact, leading wildcard, trailing wildcard, regex). Do not try to decide in a single pass.
For the wildcard passes keep the best length seen so far and replace it only when strictly longer, so that earlier servers win ties.
guide.brute_force: One loop over the servers that returns the first name matching in any way. It fails whenever a wildcard server is written before the exact one, which is the classic real-world surprise this algorithm prevents.
guide.approach:
1. Stage A: candidates with `listen == ip:port`, else those with `*:port`, else `-1`.
2. Normalise the host: lower-case, cut at `:`.
3. Pass 1: exact names (and `.x` as `x`).
4. Pass 2: suffixes from `*.x` and `.x`; keep the longest.
5. Pass 3: prefixes from `x.*`; keep the longest.
6. Pass 4: regexes in order.
7. Fallback: the flagged default, else the first candidate.

Dry run: names `*.test` (0), `*.shop.test` (1), `www.shop.*` (2), host `www.shop.test`. No exact match. Leading wildcards: `.test` (5 chars) and `.shop.test` (10 chars) both match; the longer wins → server 1. The trailing wildcard is never consulted.
guide.complexity: Time O(total number of names × host length); space O(number of servers) for the candidate list. Real NGINX uses hash tables for the first three passes.
guide.pitfalls: Forgetting stage A; treating `_` as a wildcard (it is an ordinary name); letting `*.shop.test` match `shop.test` itself; comparing case-sensitively; keeping the port in the host.
guide.follow_up: Add IPv6 listen addresses, and the rule that a request with an invalid Host header is still routed to the default server.

nginx-directive-inheritance.title: Directive Inheritance Across Levels
nginx-directive-inheritance.description:
NGINX configuration is nested: `http` contains `server`, which contains `location`. Write
`effective_config(levels, not_inherited)` that returns the directives in force at the **innermost** level.

- `levels` is a list of dictionaries from outermost to innermost. Each maps a directive name to its value: a string for
  ordinary directives, or a **list** of strings for directives that may be repeated (`add_header`, `proxy_set_header`,
  `limit_req` and so on).
- **Ordinary rule:** the innermost level that sets a directive wins.
- **Repeated directives follow the same rule and do not merge:** if an inner level sets `add_header` at all, the lists
  from outer levels are dropped entirely.
- `not_inherited` lists directives that act only at the level where they are written (`return`, `proxy_pass`,
  `try_files`, `rewrite`). They appear in the result only if the innermost level itself sets them.

Return a dictionary. Lists must be new lists with the same items in the same order.

**Example:** `[{"gzip": "on", "add_header": ["X-A 1", "X-B 2"]}, {"root": "/srv"}, {"add_header": ["X-C 3"]}]`,
`[]` → `{"gzip": "on", "root": "/srv", "add_header": ["X-C 3"]}`

guide.prereqs: Dictionaries and lists. Lesson: *Installing NGINX and reading nginx.conf* (contexts and inheritance).
guide.intuition: Walk from the outside in and let each level overwrite what it mentions. Two refinements: a list is replaced, never extended, and some directives are actions that never travel inward.
hints: Start with an empty result and process `levels` in order; later assignments overwrite earlier ones.
For a list value, assign a copy of the inner list. Do not concatenate with the outer one.
When a directive is in `not_inherited`, accept it only while processing the last level.
guide.brute_force: For every directive name appearing anywhere, scan the levels from innermost to outermost for the first one that defines it. Same answer, O(names × levels).
guide.approach:
1. `out = {}`.
2. For each level with its depth: for each directive, skip it when it is not inherited and this is not the last level; otherwise store it (copying lists).
3. Return `out`.

Dry run on the example: after level 0, `gzip=on`, `add_header=[X-A 1, X-B 2]`. Level 1 adds `root`. Level 2 sets `add_header`, replacing the list with `[X-C 3]`. The two outer headers are gone, which is exactly the trap that removes security headers in real configurations.
guide.complexity: Time O(total number of directives across levels); space O(number of distinct directives).
guide.pitfalls: Merging lists; mutating the input lists by returning the same object; dropping a not-inherited directive even when the innermost level sets it; crashing on an empty `levels`.
guide.follow_up: Recent NGINX versions let some list directives opt in to merging. Add a third argument naming directives whose lists should be concatenated.

nginx-location-match.title: Pick the Location Block
nginx-location-match.description:
Implement NGINX's location selection. `match_location(locations, uri)` returns the **index** of the location that
handles `uri`, or `-1` if none does.

Each location is `[modifier, pattern]` in configuration order. Modifiers:

| Modifier | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `"="` | exact match of the whole URI |
| `""` | prefix match |
| `"^~"` | prefix match that, when it is the longest matching prefix, stops the search |
| `"~"` | case-sensitive regular expression (`re.search`) |
| `"~*"` | case-insensitive regular expression |

Algorithm:

1. If an exact location equals the URI, it wins.
2. Among prefix locations (`""` and `"^~"`), remember the **longest** that the URI starts with.
3. If that longest prefix has `^~`, it wins.
4. Otherwise test the regex locations **in order**; the first that matches wins.
5. If no regex matches, the remembered prefix wins; with no prefix either, return `-1`.

**Example:** `[["", "/images/"], ["~", "\\.(png|jpg)$"]]`, `"/images/logo.png"` → `1`

**Example:** `[["^~", "/images/"], ["~", "\\.(png|jpg)$"]]`, `"/images/logo.png"` → `0`

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *How NGINX picks a location block*. `str.startswith`, `re.search` with `re.I`.
guide.intuition: Three kinds of location compete in a fixed order of authority: exact, then prefix, then regex, with one twist. A regex normally overrules the best prefix, unless that prefix carries `^~`, which is the author saying "do not ask the regexes".
hints: Handle the exact modifier in its own first loop and return immediately.
Find the longest matching prefix before looking at any regex, and keep its index.
Only the *longest* prefix's `^~` matters. A shorter `^~` prefix that also matches has no effect.
guide.brute_force: There is nothing cheaper than three linear passes for a list this small. The mistake to avoid is collapsing them into one pass that returns the first thing that matches.
guide.approach:
1. Pass 1: exact.
2. Pass 2: longest prefix among `""` and `"^~"`.
3. If its modifier is `^~`, return it.
4. Pass 3: regexes in file order, honouring case sensitivity.
5. Return the remembered prefix (or -1).

Dry run: locations `/a/` (0), `^~ /a/b/` (1), `~ c$` (2), `= /a/b/c` (3); URI `/a/b/cc`. No exact match. Prefixes `/a/` and `/a/b/` match; the longest is index 1, which has `^~`, so the answer is 1 and the regex at index 2, which would have matched, is never tried.
guide.complexity: Time O(L × |uri|) for L locations; space O(1). NGINX stores prefixes in a tree, so its prefix step is faster.
guide.pitfalls: Letting the longest prefix beat a matching regex; honouring `^~` on a prefix that is not the longest; choosing the longest or most specific regex instead of the first; forgetting that `/api` is a prefix of `/apiary`.
guide.follow_up: Add named locations (`@name`), which never match a URI, and model the internal redirect done by `index` so that `/` ends up in the location for `/index.html`.

nginx-try-files.title: Resolve try_files
nginx-try-files.description:
`try_files` checks a list of candidates and uses the first that exists; the **last** argument is special. Write
`try_files(files, dirs, args, uri)`.

- `files` lists existing files and `dirs` existing folders, as absolute URL paths under the site root (`"/"` is the
  root folder; other folders have no trailing slash, e.g. `"/docs"`).
- `args` are the directive's arguments, at least one. The text `$uri` inside an argument is replaced by `uri`.

For every argument **except the last**, in order:

- If it ends with `/`, it asks for a **folder**: strip the trailing slashes (an empty result means `"/"`). If that
  folder exists, return `["dir", folder]`.
- Otherwise it asks for a **file**: if it exists, return `["file", path]`.

If none exists, the last argument is a **fallback** that is used without any existence check:

- `=CODE` → `["status", CODE]` with CODE as an integer,
- `@name` → `["named", "@name"]`,
- anything else → `["redirect", path]`, an internal redirect to that URI.

**Example:** files `["/index.html", "/app.js"]`, dirs `["/"]`, args `["$uri", "$uri/", "/index.html"]`:
`"/app.js"` → `["file", "/app.js"]`; `"/tea/oolong"` → `["redirect", "/index.html"]`

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *try_files, return, rewrite and the proxy_pass slash*. Sets for fast membership tests.
guide.intuition: Every argument but the last is a question ("does this exist?"). The last is an instruction ("then do this"), carried out without asking. A trailing slash turns a question about a file into a question about a folder.
hints: Slice the list: loop over `args[:-1]`, then treat `args[-1]` separately.
A path ending in `/` must be looked up in `dirs`, never in `files`.
The fallback is not checked for existence. `/index.html` as the last argument produces a redirect even if the file is missing.
guide.brute_force: Check each candidate against the lists with `in` on a list: O(n) per check. Converting to sets first makes each check O(1).
guide.approach:
1. Build sets.
2. For each non-final argument substitute `$uri`; branch on the trailing slash; return on the first hit.
3. Classify the final argument by its first character.

Dry run: args `$uri $uri/ =404`, URI `/docs`, files `/docs/a.html`, dirs `/`, `/docs`. Candidate 1 `/docs` is not a file. Candidate 2 `/docs/` → folder `/docs` exists → `["dir", "/docs"]`. In NGINX the index module then looks for an index file inside it.
guide.complexity: Time O(len(args) + len(files) + len(dirs)); space O(len(files) + len(dirs)).
guide.pitfalls: Checking the fallback for existence; treating `=404` in the middle of the list as special; accepting a folder for a file candidate; mishandling the root URI `/`, whose folder candidate is `//`.
guide.follow_up: Model the loop: when the fallback redirects to a URI that again falls through to the same fallback, NGINX stops after ten rounds with a 500. Detect that.

nginx-proxy-pass-uri.title: The proxy_pass Trailing Slash
nginx-proxy-pass-uri.description:
Given a prefix `location`, the value of `proxy_pass`, and the client's request URI, return the URI that NGINX sends to
the upstream server.

- If `proxy_pass` has **no URI part**, meaning nothing after the host and optional port, the request URI is passed
  unchanged.
- If it **has a URI part**, even a single `/`, the part of the path matched by the location prefix is replaced by that
  URI part.
- The query string (from `?` on) is always kept as it is.

You may assume the request path starts with `location`.

**Example:** `"/app/"`, `"http://backend/"`, `"/app/users?id=7"` → `"/users?id=7"`

**Example:** `"/app/"`, `"http://backend"`, `"/app/users?id=7"` → `"/app/users?id=7"`

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *try_files, return, rewrite and the proxy_pass slash*. `str.partition`.
guide.intuition: NGINX asks one question: did the author write a path on `proxy_pass`? No path means "send what you received". A path means "swap the matched prefix for my path", and a lone slash is a path.
hints: Separate the query string first with `partition("?")` and glue it back at the end.
Remove the scheme with `split("://", 1)`, then `partition("/")` tells you whether a URI part exists and what it is.
The replacement is plain string surgery: URI part + the path after the location prefix. Do not add or remove slashes.
guide.brute_force: Not applicable; this is constant-time string handling. The naive mistake is `str.replace(location, ...)`, which also rewrites later occurrences of the prefix inside the path or the query.
guide.approach:
1. `path, mark, query = request_uri.partition("?")`.
2. `host, slash, uri_part = after_scheme.partition("/")`.
3. If `slash` is empty return the original. Otherwise new path = `"/" + uri_part + path[len(location):]`.

Dry run: location `/app/`, `http://backend/v2`, request `/app/users`. URI part is `v2`; the path after the prefix is `users`; result `/v2users`. That missing slash is a real and common bug, and the function reproduces it faithfully.
guide.complexity: Time and space O(length of the URI).
guide.pitfalls: Normalising slashes (NGINX does not); losing the query string; treating a port (`:8000`) as a URI part; using `replace`, which may touch the query.
guide.follow_up: When `proxy_pass` contains variables, or the location is a regex, NGINX cannot do the replacement and passes the URI as given. Add a flag for that case.

nginx-rewrite-eval.title: Evaluate rewrite and return Directives
nginx-rewrite-eval.description:
Simulate the rewrite module for a list of directives written at one level. `rewrite_eval(directives, uri)` returns
`[status, uri_or_url]`. The URI has no query string in this problem.

Directives are processed in order. Each is one of:

- `["return", code, text]`: stop immediately and return `[code, text]`, with every `$uri` in `text` replaced by the
  **current** URI.
- `["rewrite", regex, replacement, flag]`: if `re.search(regex, uri)` finds nothing, go on to the next directive.
  Otherwise build the new value from `replacement`, replacing `$1`..`$9` with the regex groups (a group that does not
  exist or did not take part becomes the empty string). Then:
  - if the new value starts with `http://` or `https://`: return `[301, value]` when the flag is `"permanent"`,
    otherwise `[302, value]`;
  - flag `"permanent"`: return `[301, value]`; flag `"redirect"`: return `[302, value]`;
  - otherwise the URI becomes the new value. With flag `"last"` or `"break"` processing stops; with the empty flag
    `""` it continues with the next directive.

If processing ends without a redirect or a `return`, the answer is `[200, current_uri]`.

**Example:** `[["rewrite", "^/old/(.*)$", "/new/$1", "last"], ["return", 404, ""]]`, `"/old/page"` → `[200, "/new/page"]`

**Example:** the same directives with `"/other"` → `[404, ""]`

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *try_files, return, rewrite and the proxy_pass slash*. Regular expression groups.
guide.intuition: The rewrite module is a tiny program run top to bottom with one register, the current URI. `rewrite` may change the register and may stop the program; `return` always stops it and answers the client.
hints: Keep one variable for the current URI and update it after each successful internal rewrite; later directives must see the new value.
Decide redirects before flags: a replacement beginning with a scheme is a redirect whatever the flag says.
Both `last` and `break` end this list of directives. Only the empty flag lets processing continue.
guide.brute_force: There is no asymptotically different approach; the work is in getting the control flow exactly right. Writing the four outcomes as an explicit if-chain is clearer than trying to be clever.
guide.approach:
1. Loop over the directives.
2. `return`: substitute `$uri`, answer.
3. `rewrite`: search; on a match expand `$1`..`$9`; check for an absolute URL, then `permanent`, then `redirect`; otherwise assign and stop on `last` or `break`.
4. After the loop answer `[200, uri]`.

Dry run: `/a` through `^/a$→/b`, `^/b$→/c`, `^/c$→/d break`, `^/d$→/e`. The URI becomes `/b`, `/c`, `/d`, and `break` stops before the fourth rule: `[200, "/d"]`.
guide.complexity: Time O(number of directives × cost of each regex search); space O(length of the URI).
guide.pitfalls: Matching against the original URI instead of the current one; continuing after `last`; treating only the `redirect` flag as a redirect and missing absolute URLs; crashing on `$2` when the regex has one group.
guide.follow_up: In a real server `last` restarts location matching and `break` does not. Combine this function with `match_location` and stop after ten rounds with a 500, as NGINX does.

nginx-smooth-wrr.title: Smooth Weighted Round Robin
nginx-smooth-wrr.description:
NGINX's default balancing method is **smooth weighted round robin**. With weights 5, 1, 1 a naive scheme would send
five requests in a row to the first server. The smooth version spreads them: `a a b a c a a`.

Write `smooth_wrr(weights, n)` returning the list of server indices chosen for `n` consecutive requests.

Algorithm, per request:

1. Every server keeps a number `current`, starting at 0. Add each server's `weight` to its `current`.
2. Choose the server with the largest `current` (the lowest index wins ties).
3. Subtract the **sum of all weights** from the chosen server's `current`.

Weights are positive integers. If `weights` is empty, return an empty list.

**Example:** `[5, 1, 1]`, `7` → `[0, 0, 1, 0, 2, 0, 0]`

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *HTTP load balancing and the balancing methods*. Lists and loops.
guide.intuition: Each server earns credit at a rate equal to its weight. Whoever holds the most credit serves the next request and pays the price of one full round. Heavy servers earn quickly and are picked often, but paying the full round each time stops them from being picked many times in a row.
hints: Keep one integer per server and update all of them on every request.
The amount subtracted is the same for every server: the sum of all weights.
On ties, keep the earlier server. Compare with a strict `>` while scanning from index 0.
guide.brute_force: Expand the weights into a list such as `[0,0,0,0,0,1,2]` and cycle through it. The proportions are right over a full cycle, but the heavy server receives bursts, which is exactly what the smooth algorithm was introduced to avoid.
guide.approach:
1. `total = sum(weights)`, `current = [0] * k`.
2. For each request add the weights, find the arg-max, subtract `total` from it, record it.

Dry run with `[5,1,1]` (total 7): currents become `[5,1,1]` → pick 0 → `[-2,1,1]`. Add → `[3,2,2]` → pick 0 → `[-4,2,2]`. Add → `[1,3,3]` → pick 1 (tie with 2, lower index) → `[1,-4,3]`. Add → `[6,-3,4]` → 0. Add → `[4,-2,5]` → 2. Then 0, 0, and the currents are back to all zeros: the pattern repeats every 7 requests.
guide.complexity: Time O(n × k) for k servers; space O(k) besides the output.
guide.pitfalls: Subtracting the chosen server's own weight instead of the total; breaking ties towards the later server; dividing by zero or indexing an empty list.
guide.follow_up: NGINX lowers a server's *effective* weight after failures and lets it recover gradually. Add an `effective` array that is used in place of `weights` and adjusted on failure.

nginx-least-conn.title: Least Connections with Weights
nginx-least-conn.description:
The `least_conn` method sends each new request to the server with the fewest requests in progress, taking weights into
account. Write `least_conn(weights, events)` and return the server index chosen for each request, in order.

`events` is a list in time order:

- `["req", id]`: a new request arrives and must be assigned.
- `["done", id]`: that request has finished and no longer counts. An unknown id is ignored.

A server's load is `active / weight`, where `active` is its number of requests in progress. Choose the server with the
**smallest load**; on a tie choose the lowest index. Compare loads without floating point: server `i` is strictly less
loaded than server `j` when `active[i] * weight[j] < active[j] * weight[i]`.

**Example:** weights `[1, 1]`, events `[["req","a"], ["req","b"], ["done","a"], ["req","c"]]` → `[0, 1, 0]`

**Example:** weights `[2, 1]`, three requests and no completions → `[0, 1, 0]`

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *HTTP load balancing and the balancing methods*. Dictionaries.
guide.intuition: Round robin counts requests handed out. Least connections counts requests still running, so a server stuck on slow requests stops receiving new ones until it catches up. Weights scale the comparison: a server with weight 2 is allowed twice as many before it looks equally busy.
hints: You need two pieces of state: how many requests each server has in progress, and which server each request id went to.
Cross-multiply to compare `a/b` with `c/d` using integers only.
Use a strict `<` while scanning upward so that the lowest index wins ties.
guide.brute_force: Compute `active[i] / weights[i]` as floats and take the minimum. It works for small numbers; cross-multiplication avoids any rounding doubt and is no harder.
guide.approach:
1. `active = [0]*k`, `placed = {}`.
2. On `req`: scan for the least loaded server, increment it, remember `placed[id]`, record the index.
3. On `done`: look up the id, decrement that server, forget the id.

Dry run with weights `[2,1]`: first request, loads 0 and 0, tie → 0. Second: loads 1/2 and 0 → 1. Third: 1/2 against 1/1 → 0. Result `[0,1,0]`.
guide.complexity: Time O(events × servers); space O(servers + requests in progress).
guide.pitfalls: Ignoring weights; never decrementing; decrementing twice for a repeated `done`; breaking ties towards the last server.
guide.follow_up: Real NGINX breaks ties with weighted round robin instead of the lowest index. Combine this with `smooth_wrr` over the tied servers.

nginx-hash-select.title: ip_hash: Choose a Server from the Client Address
nginx-hash-select.description:
With `ip_hash`, NGINX sends all requests from one client network to the same server. Reproduce its calculation.

`ip_hash(ips, weights, down)` returns, for each IPv4 address in `ips`, the index of the chosen server. `weights` are
the servers' weights and `down` is a list of indices that are currently unavailable.

For one address:

1. Take only the **first three octets** (so a whole /24 network maps to one server).
2. Start with `hash = 89`. For each of the three octets in order: `hash = (hash * 113 + octet) % 6271`.
3. `w = hash % total_weight`. Walk the servers from index 0: while `w >= weight` of the current server, subtract that
   weight from `w` and move to the next server. The server you stop on is the candidate.
4. If the candidate is not in `down`, it is the answer. If it is, **repeat steps 2 and 3 without resetting `hash`**
   (feed the same three octets in again) and test the new candidate. After 20 unsuccessful attempts the answer is `-1`.

**Example:** `["203.0.113.5", "203.0.113.200"]`, weights `[1, 1, 1]`, no servers down → both get the same index.
nginx-hash-select.solution:
def ip_hash(ips, weights, down):
    total = sum(weights)
    unavailable = set(down)
    out = []
    for ip in ips:
        octets = [int(x) for x in ip.split(".")[:3]]
        h = 89
        chosen = -1
        for _ in range(20):
            for o in octets:
                h = (h * 113 + o) % 6271
            w = h % total
            idx = 0
            while w >= weights[idx]:
                w -= weights[idx]
                idx += 1
            if idx not in unavailable:
                chosen = idx
                break
        out.append(chosen)
    return out

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *HTTP load balancing and the balancing methods* (ip_hash). The `%` operator.
guide.intuition: A hash turns the address into a number that looks random but is always the same for the same input. Reducing that number modulo the total weight and walking the weights converts it into a server, with heavier servers covering more of the range.
hints: Split on dots and keep three numbers. The fourth octet must not influence the result.
The walk in step 3 is the standard way to pick from weighted items: subtract weights until the remainder fits.
For the retry, do not start again from 89. Continue from the current hash value, which is why the next candidate differs.
guide.brute_force: A simpler but different scheme is `sum(octets) % number_of_servers`. It ignores weights and clusters badly; it is not what NGINX does, so its answers do not match.
guide.approach:
1. Precompute `total` and a set of down servers.
2. For each address: three octets, `h = 89`.
3. Up to 20 times: fold the octets into `h`, compute `w`, walk the weights, accept if available.

Dry run for `10.0.0.1` with weights `[1,1,1]`: h = (89·113+10) % 6271 = 3796; then (3796·113+0) % 6271 = 2520; then (2520·113+0) % 6271 = 2565. `w = 2565 % 3 = 0` → server 0.
guide.complexity: Time O(addresses × (tries × servers)); space O(servers).
guide.pitfalls: Using all four octets; resetting the hash on retry (which would pick the same down server twenty times); an off-by-one in the weight walk; returning a server that is down.
guide.follow_up: `hash $key consistent;` uses a ring so that removing a server remaps only that server's keys. Implement a consistent-hash ring with 160 points per unit of weight and measure how many keys move when one server leaves.

nginx-passive-health.title: Passive Health Checks: max_fails and fail_timeout
nginx-passive-health.description:
Open-source NGINX judges an upstream server by the requests it sends there. Simulate one server with the parameters
`max_fails` and `fail_timeout` (seconds).

`passive_health(max_fails, fail_timeout, events)` receives `events`, a list of `[time, would_succeed]` in increasing
time order. Each is a moment at which NGINX would like to use the server, and whether the server would answer
correctly at that moment. Return one string per event:

- `"skipped"` if the server is currently marked unavailable. No request is sent, so nothing is learned.
- `"ok"` if a request is sent and succeeds.
- `"fail"` if a request is sent and fails.

Rules for this model:

- A failure at time `t` is remembered while `now - t < fail_timeout`.
- When a new failure brings the number of remembered failures to `max_fails`, the server is marked unavailable from
  that moment until `now + fail_timeout` (exclusive), and the remembered failures are cleared.
- At or after that time the server is tried again as normal.
- `max_fails = 0` switches the mechanism off: the server is never skipped.
- A success does not erase remembered failures; they expire with time.

**Example:** `max_fails=2`, `fail_timeout=10`, events `[[0,False],[1,False],[5,True],[11,True]]`
→ `["fail", "fail", "skipped", "ok"]`
nginx-passive-health.solution:
def passive_health(max_fails, fail_timeout, events):
    fails = []
    unavailable_until = None
    out = []
    for t, would_succeed in events:
        if unavailable_until is not None and t < unavailable_until:
            out.append("skipped")
            continue
        if would_succeed:
            out.append("ok")
            continue
        out.append("fail")
        fails = [f for f in fails if t - f < fail_timeout]
        fails.append(t)
        if max_fails > 0 and len(fails) >= max_fails:
            unavailable_until = t + fail_timeout
            fails = []
    return out

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *Health checks, retries, draining and slow start*. Lists and conditionals.
guide.intuition: `fail_timeout` plays two roles: it is the window in which failures are counted and the length of the time-out once the count is reached. While a server is in time-out NGINX sends it nothing, so it cannot learn whether the server recovered until the time-out ends and a real request is risked.
hints: Check the unavailable period first. A skipped event must not change any state.
Before adding a failure, drop the ones that are `fail_timeout` or more seconds old.
Handle `max_fails = 0` explicitly, or zero failures would satisfy `>= 0` at once.
guide.brute_force: Count failures for ever with a single integer. It gives the same answer only when failures arrive close together; two failures an hour apart would wrongly disable a server configured with `max_fails=2 fail_timeout=10s`.
guide.approach:
1. State: a list of recent failure times and `unavailable_until`.
2. For each event: skipped if inside the unavailable period; `ok` if it would succeed; otherwise `fail`, prune old failures, append, and if the count reaches `max_fails` set `unavailable_until = t + fail_timeout` and clear the list.

Dry run of the example: t=0 fail (1 remembered), t=1 fail (2 → unavailable until 11), t=5 skipped even though the server has recovered, t=11 tried again → ok.
guide.complexity: Time O(events × max_fails) because the remembered list never exceeds `max_fails` entries; space O(max_fails).
guide.pitfalls: Counting failures outside the window; changing state on skipped events; forgetting that the boundary `t == unavailable_until` is available again; letting `max_fails = 0` disable the server.
guide.follow_up: Extend to several servers with round robin and `proxy_next_upstream`: a failed attempt is retried on the next available server, and when all are unavailable the client receives 502.

nginx-map-eval.title: Evaluate a map Block
nginx-map-eval.description:
A `map` block computes one variable from another by looking it up in a table. Write `map_eval(entries, source)` that
returns the resulting value.

`entries` is a list of `[pattern, value]` in configuration order. A pattern is one of:

- the word `default`: the value used when nothing else matches (if there is no `default` entry, the result is `""`);
- a **regular expression**: starts with `~` (case-sensitive) or `~*` (case-insensitive); test the rest with
  `re.search`;
- anything else: a **plain string**, compared with the source **ignoring letter case**. The empty string `""` is a
  valid plain pattern and matches an empty source.

Order of evaluation, whatever the order in the file:

1. plain strings (an exact match wins immediately),
2. regular expressions, in the order they are written; the first that matches wins,
3. the default.

**Example:** `[["default", "0"], ["~^5", "1"], ["503", "skip"]]`: source `"503"` → `"skip"`; `"502"` → `"1"`;
`"200"` → `"0"`

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *A/B testing, map, geo and finding the real client*. `re.search` and the `re.I` flag.
guide.intuition: A `map` is a lookup table with three tiers of authority. An exact string is the most specific statement and always wins. Regular expressions are tried next in the order written. The default catches the rest. Position in the file matters only among the regexes.
hints: Make three passes over the entries instead of one.
Plain strings are compared without regard to case; regexes follow their own `~` or `~*` marker.
Find the default in advance, because it may be written anywhere in the block.
guide.brute_force: One pass that returns the first entry that matches in any way. It breaks as soon as a regex is written above an exact string that it also matches, as in the first example.
guide.approach:
1. Scan for `default`.
2. Scan plain strings for a case-insensitive equal.
3. Scan regexes in order.
4. Return the default.

Dry run of `[default→0, ~^5→1, 503→skip]` with `503`: pass 1 finds the default `0`. Pass 2 finds the plain string `503` → `skip`. The regex `^5`, written earlier in the file, is never consulted.
guide.complexity: Time O(entries × cost of a regex search); space O(1). NGINX stores the plain strings in a hash table, making pass 2 constant time.
guide.pitfalls: Using file order for everything; case-sensitive comparison of plain strings; applying `re.I` to `~` patterns; returning `None` instead of the empty string when there is no default.
guide.follow_up: Add the `hostnames` parameter, which enables wildcard patterns such as `*.example.com` evaluated between the plain strings and the regexes.

nginx-split-clients.title: split_clients: Percentage Buckets
nginx-split-clients.description:
`split_clients` assigns each request to a variant for A/B testing. It hashes a key to a 32-bit number and compares the
number with cumulative percentage thresholds. Write the comparison part.

`split_clients(buckets, hash_value)`:

- `buckets` is a list of `[percent, value]` in order. `percent` is a string such as `"10%"` or `"0.5%"` with at most
  two decimal places, or `"*"` meaning "everything that is left".
- `hash_value` is an integer from 0 to 4294967295 (`0xffffffff`).

Go through the buckets in order, keeping a running total of the percentages in **hundredths of a percent** (so `10%`
is 1000 and `0.5%` is 50). For each bucket:

- if its percent is `"*"`, return its value;
- otherwise add it to the total and compute `threshold = total * 4294967295 // 10000` with integer arithmetic; if
  `hash_value < threshold`, return its value.

If no bucket is chosen, return `""`.

**Example:** `[["10%", "a"], ["0.5%", "b"], ["*", "c"]]`: hash `0` → `"a"`; hash `440000000` → `"b"`;
hash `4000000000` → `"c"`

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *A/B testing, map, geo and finding the real client*. Integer division.
guide.intuition: Lay the whole range of 32-bit numbers out as a ruler. Each bucket claims the next stretch of it, as long as its percentage. A request's hash is a point on the ruler, and the bucket whose stretch contains the point wins. Because the hash of a given key never changes, a user stays in the same bucket.
hints: Thresholds are cumulative: the second bucket's threshold uses the sum of the first two percentages.
Work in hundredths of a percent so that `0.5%` is the integer 50 and no fractions are compared.
Use `round(...)` when converting, since `33.33 * 100` is not exactly 3333 in floating point.
guide.brute_force: Reduce the hash with `% 100` and compare with whole percentages. It cannot represent `0.5%`, and it uses only the low digits of the hash. NGINX compares against the full 32-bit range.
guide.approach:
1. `total = 0`.
2. For each bucket: `*` returns at once; otherwise add its hundredths, compute the threshold, compare.
3. Fall through to `""`.

Dry run with `10%`, `0.5%`, `*` and hash 440000000: threshold 1 = 1000 × 4294967295 // 10000 = 429496729, and the hash is not below it. Threshold 2 = 1050 × 4294967295 // 10000 = 450971565, and the hash is below it → `b`.
guide.complexity: Time O(number of buckets); space O(1).
guide.pitfalls: Comparing against each bucket's own percentage instead of the running total; using `<=`; float rounding when parsing; assuming percentages that sum to 100 cover every hash (the largest hash value, 4294967295, is not below the final threshold, a real quirk of the integer arithmetic).
guide.follow_up: NGINX hashes the key with MurmurHash2. Implement that hash and verify that about 10% of 100,000 random keys fall in a `10%` bucket.

nginx-limit-conn.title: limit_conn: Cap Simultaneous Connections per Key
nginx-limit-conn.description:
`limit_conn zone N;` allows at most `N` requests in progress at the same moment for each key (usually the client
address). Write `limit_conn(limit, events)`.

`events` is a list in time order:

- `["open", conn_id, key]`: a request starts. Decide `"pass"` or `"reject"`.
- `["close", conn_id]`: that request ends.

Rules:

- A request is rejected when its key already has `limit` requests in progress. A rejected request is **not counted**
  and its later `close` event changes nothing.
- A request whose key is the empty string is always passed and never counted.
- A `close` for an unknown `conn_id` is ignored.

Return the list of verdicts for the `open` events, in order.

**Example:** `limit=2`, events `[["open",1,"a"], ["open",2,"a"], ["open",3,"a"], ["close",1], ["open",4,"a"]]`
→ `["pass", "pass", "reject", "pass"]`

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *Limiting request rate, connections and bandwidth*. Dictionaries.
guide.intuition: This is a counter per key that goes up when a request starts and down when it ends. The only subtlety is bookkeeping: a rejected request never entered, so it must not be counted on the way in or on the way out.
hints: Keep two dictionaries: key → current count, and connection id → key (for accepted requests only).
Decide before incrementing: reject when the count is already at the limit.
On close, look the connection up; if it is not there it was rejected, exempt or unknown, so do nothing.
guide.brute_force: Keep a list of open connections and count those with the same key on every `open`: O(n) per event. The dictionary of counts makes it O(1).
guide.approach:
1. `counts = {}`, `owner = {}`.
2. `open`: empty key → pass. Count at limit → reject. Otherwise count up, remember the owner, pass.
3. `close`: pop the owner; if found, count down.

Dry run of the example with limit 2: opens 1 and 2 pass (count 2). Open 3 is rejected and not recorded. Close 1 brings the count to 1. Open 4 passes.
guide.complexity: Time O(number of events); space O(open connections + distinct keys).
guide.pitfalls: Counting rejected requests, which makes the key stay over the limit for ever; decrementing on the close of a rejected request; counting the empty key; forgetting that `limit=0` rejects everything with a non-empty key.
guide.follow_up: Apply two zones at once, per address and per virtual server, and reject if either is full, as in `limit_conn perip 10; limit_conn perserver 500;`.

nginx-limit-req.title: limit_req: the Leaky Bucket with burst and nodelay
nginx-limit-req.description:
Implement NGINX's request rate limiter for one zone. `limit_req(rate, burst, nodelay, requests)`:

- `rate`: allowed requests per second (a positive integer).
- `burst`: how many requests above the rate may be accepted (0 or more).
- `nodelay`: `True` to forward accepted requests at once, `False` to delay them so that they leave at the rate.
- `requests`: a list of `[key, time_ms]` in increasing time order.

Return one `[verdict, delay_ms]` per request, where the verdict is `"pass"` or `"reject"`.

NGINX keeps, per key, an integer `excess` in **thousandths of a request** and the time of the last accepted request:

- A key seen for the first time: store `excess = 0`, answer `["pass", 0]`.
- Otherwise compute `excess = max(0, stored_excess - rate * (now - last) + 1000)`, with times in milliseconds.
  - If `excess > burst * 1000`: answer `["reject", 0]` and **leave the stored state unchanged**.
  - Else store the new `excess` and `now`, and answer `["pass", delay]` where `delay` is `0` with `nodelay` and
    `excess // rate` milliseconds without it.
- A request with the empty string as key is not limited: `["pass", 0]`, and nothing is stored.

**Example:** `rate=5, burst=0`, one key at times `0, 1, 200` → `pass, reject, pass` (5 r/s means one per 200 ms)

**Example:** `rate=5, burst=3, nodelay=False`, one key at `0, 0, 0` → delays `0, 200, 400`

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *Limiting request rate, connections and bandwidth*. Integer arithmetic and dictionaries.
guide.intuition: Picture a bucket per client. Each request adds one unit; the bucket leaks `rate` units per second. `excess` is the level after adding the new request. If the level would rise above `burst`, the request is refused and the bucket is left as it was. Working in thousandths keeps everything in integers, as NGINX does.
hints: With times in milliseconds and excess in thousandths, the leak since the last accepted request is `rate * (now - last)` with no division.
Add the new request (1000) before clamping at zero, not after.
A rejected request must not update the stored excess or the stored time, or a client that keeps hammering would never be let back in.
guide.brute_force: Count requests per key in fixed one-second windows and reject above `rate + burst`. It is simple and behaves differently: it allows a double burst across a window boundary and cannot express "one per 200 ms".
guide.approach:
1. `state[key] = (excess, last_ms)`.
2. Empty key → pass, untouched state.
3. New key → store `(0, now)`, pass.
4. Else compute the new excess; compare with `burst * 1000`; reject without storing, or store and compute the delay.

Dry run, `rate=5, burst=0`, times 0, 1, 200: first request stores excess 0. At 1 ms: `0 - 5·1 + 1000 = 995 > 0` → reject, state unchanged. At 200 ms: `0 - 5·200 + 1000 = 0`, not above 0 → pass.
guide.complexity: Time O(number of requests); space O(number of distinct keys).
guide.pitfalls: Updating state on rejection; clamping before adding the request, which makes `burst=0` reject every request after the first; using `>=` for the comparison; forgetting the exempt empty key; floating-point drift.
guide.follow_up: Add the `delay=N` parameter: the first N excess requests pass without delay and later ones are delayed by `(excess - N*1000) // rate` milliseconds.

nginx-cache-control-ttl.title: How Long May NGINX Cache This Response?
nginx-cache-control-ttl.description:
When a proxied response arrives, NGINX decides whether to store it and for how many seconds. Write
`cache_ttl(status, headers, valid)` returning that number of seconds, where `0` means "do not cache".

- `status` is the upstream's status code.
- `headers` maps **lower-case** response header names to their values.
- `valid` holds the `proxy_cache_valid` settings: keys are status codes as strings (`"200"`) or `"any"`, values are
  seconds.

Apply these rules in order and stop at the first that decides:

1. A `set-cookie` header, or `vary` equal to `*`, means **0**.
2. `x-accel-expires`: its integer value is the answer (0 disables caching). Nothing below is consulted.
3. `cache-control`: split it on commas and ignore case and surrounding spaces.
   - `no-cache`, `no-store` or `private` → **0**;
   - otherwise `s-maxage=N` → `N`; if there is no `s-maxage`, `max-age=N` → `N`.
4. Otherwise use `valid`: the entry for this status, else the entry `"any"`, else **0**.

(The `Expires` header is left out of this problem.)

**Example:** `200`, `{"cache-control": "public, max-age=60"}`, `{"200": 600}` → `60`

**Example:** `200`, `{}`, `{"200": 600}` → `600`

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *Proxy caching: zones, keys and validity*. Dictionaries and string splitting.
guide.intuition: The application knows its data best, so its response headers outrank the proxy's blanket `proxy_cache_valid` rules. Among the headers there is a pecking order too: a private signal for the proxy (`X-Accel-Expires`), then the public `Cache-Control`. Anything that marks the response as personal vetoes caching outright.
hints: Deal with the vetoes first: `Set-Cookie` and `Vary: *`.
Look for `s-maxage` across all parts before looking for `max-age`; their order inside the header must not matter.
`proxy_cache_valid` is the fallback, not the first choice.
guide.brute_force: No cheaper approach exists; the task is a fixed sequence of checks. The usual mistake is collapsing them, for example scanning the `Cache-Control` parts once and returning on the first of `max-age` or `s-maxage` seen.
guide.approach:
1. Vetoes → 0.
2. `x-accel-expires` → its value.
3. Parse `cache-control` into clean lower-case parts; forbidden words → 0; then `s-maxage`, then `max-age`.
4. `valid[status]`, `valid['any']`, 0.

Dry run: status 200, `cache-control: max-age=60, s-maxage=300`, valid `{200: 600}`. No veto, no accel header. Parts: `max-age=60`, `s-maxage=300`. `s-maxage` is searched first → 300. The configured 600 is never used.
guide.complexity: Time O(length of the Cache-Control header); space O(number of its parts).
guide.pitfalls: Letting `proxy_cache_valid` win; preferring `max-age` because it is written first; case-sensitive matching; treating `max-age=0` as a positive lifetime; caching responses that set cookies.
guide.follow_up: Add `proxy_ignore_headers`: a list of header names whose effect is switched off, which is how people cache responses whose applications send unhelpful headers.

nginx-cache-decision.title: Cache Status: MISS, HIT, EXPIRED, STALE, BYPASS
nginx-cache-decision.description:
Simulate a proxy cache and report the cache status of every request.

`cache_sim(ttl, stale_on_error, requests)`:

- `ttl`: seconds a stored response stays fresh.
- `stale_on_error`: `True` when `proxy_cache_use_stale error timeout ...;` is configured.
- `requests`: a list in time order of `[time, method, scheme, host, uri, upstream_up, bypass]`.

For each request:

1. Only `GET` and `HEAD` are cacheable. Any other method → `"-"` (passed straight through, cache untouched).
2. The cache key is `scheme + host + uri`, with the **host lower-cased** and the URI (including any query string) kept
   exactly as given. `GET` and `HEAD` share entries.
3. If `bypass` is true (the `proxy_cache_bypass` condition holds): the response is fetched from the upstream. If the
   upstream is up, the answer is stored (replacing any entry, stamped with this time) and the status is `"BYPASS"`;
   if it is down → `"ERROR"`.
4. No entry for the key: upstream up → store, `"MISS"`; upstream down → `"ERROR"`.
5. Entry present and `time - stored_time < ttl` → `"HIT"`.
6. Entry present but expired: upstream up → store again, `"EXPIRED"`; upstream down → `"STALE"` if `stale_on_error`
   (the old entry is served and kept), otherwise `"ERROR"`.

Return the list of statuses.

**Example:** `ttl=10`, `stale_on_error=True`, three `GET https shop.test /p` requests at times 0, 5 and 12 with the
upstream up → `["MISS", "HIT", "EXPIRED"]`

guide.prereqs: Lessons: *Proxy caching: zones, keys and validity* and *Bypass, purge, locking, stale content and slicing*.
guide.intuition: A cache is a dictionary from key to stored response, plus a clock. Every status name answers two questions: was there an entry, and was it fresh? The extra cases are deliberate skips (BYPASS) and what to do when the upstream cannot refresh an expired entry (STALE or an error).
hints: Build the key exactly as specified: the query string is part of it and the host is case-insensitive.
Store only the time at which the entry was saved; freshness is `time - stored < ttl`.
A STALE answer does not refresh the entry. The next request finds it expired again.
guide.brute_force: Keep a list of all past requests and search backwards for the last time the key was stored: O(n) per request. A dictionary makes it O(1).
guide.approach:
Write the branches in the order of the statement: method, bypass, no entry, fresh, expired with upstream, expired without.

Dry run with `ttl=10`, stale serving on: t=0 → MISS (stored at 0). t=20, upstream down → entry is 20 s old, expired, cannot refresh → STALE. t=25, still down → STALE. t=30, upstream back → EXPIRED, stored at 30. t=31, upstream down again → 1 s old → HIT; the outage is invisible.
guide.complexity: Time O(number of requests); space O(number of distinct keys).
guide.pitfalls: Dropping the query string from the key, which serves page 1 for page 2; caching POST; refreshing the timestamp on a STALE answer; using `<=` at the freshness boundary; not storing the response fetched during a bypass.
guide.follow_up: Add `proxy_cache_min_uses N` (store only after N requests for a key) and `proxy_cache_lock` (concurrent misses for one key produce a single upstream fetch).

nginx-config-lint.title: A Small Configuration Linter
nginx-config-lint.description:
Pipelines run cheap checks on configuration before it reaches a server. Write `config_lint(lines)` that inspects a
configuration given as a list of text lines and returns a list of findings `[line_number, code]`, with line numbers
starting at 1, sorted by line number and then by code.

The input follows a simplified layout: at most one directive per line; a block opens on a line that ends with `{`; a
block closes on a line that contains only `}`. Everything from a `#` to the end of a line is a comment. Blank lines
and comment-only lines are ignored.

Report:

| Code | When |
|---|---|
| `MISSING_SEMICOLON` | a directive line (not a block opener, not `}`) does not end with `;` |
| `UNEXPECTED_CLOSE` | a `}` appears when no block is open (it is then ignored for the depth count) |
| `UNCLOSED_BLOCK` | at the end, at least one block is still open; report it **once**, with the number of the last line |
| `URI_IN_REDIRECT` | a line whose first word is `return` or `rewrite` uses the variable `$uri` or `$document_uri` |

About the last rule: `$uri` holds the decoded path, so placing it in a redirect lets an attacker inject line breaks
into response headers. `$request_uri` is the safe choice and must not be flagged, nor may longer names that merely
start the same way, such as `$uri_suffix`.

**Example:** `["server {", "    listen 80", "    return 301 https://$host$uri;", "}"]`
→ `[[2, "MISSING_SEMICOLON"], [3, "URI_IN_REDIRECT"]]`

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *Configuration management, templating and the API* (linting in a pipeline). String methods and a little regex.
guide.intuition: A linter is a loop with a small amount of memory. Here the memory is one number, the nesting depth. Each line is cleaned of comments and then classified as opener, closer or directive; each class has its own check.
hints: Remove the comment first, then strip whitespace; only then test what the line ends with.
Track depth with a counter: +1 for an opener, -1 for a closer, but never below zero.
For the variable check, make sure the character after `$uri` is not a letter, digit or underscore.
guide.brute_force: A real parser would tokenise the whole file, handling quotes and several directives per line. For the simplified layout that is unnecessary, and line-by-line classification is both shorter and easier to get right.
guide.approach:
1. For each line with its number: cut at `#`, strip, skip if empty.
2. If it starts with `return` or `rewrite` and contains the risky variable, record `URI_IN_REDIRECT`.
3. `}`: depth 0 → `UNEXPECTED_CLOSE`, else depth - 1. Ends with `{`: depth + 1. Otherwise, no `;` at the end → `MISSING_SEMICOLON`.
4. After the loop, depth > 0 → `UNCLOSED_BLOCK` on the last line.
5. Sort.

Dry run of the example: line 1 opens (depth 1). Line 2 `listen 80` lacks a semicolon. Line 3 is a `return` with `$uri` followed by `;` → flagged. Line 4 closes (depth 0).
guide.complexity: Time O(total characters); space O(number of findings).
guide.pitfalls: Testing the raw line so that a trailing comment hides a missing semicolon; flagging `$request_uri` or `$uri_suffix`; letting the depth go negative, which then cancels a later unclosed block; reporting `UNCLOSED_BLOCK` once per open block.
guide.follow_up: Add a rule for `proxy_pass` with a hostname but no `resolver` in the file, and one for `add_header` inside a location when the enclosing server also has `add_header` lines.

nginx-basic-auth.title: HTTP Basic Authentication Against an htpasswd File
nginx-basic-auth.description:
Implement the check behind `auth_basic`. `basic_auth(header, htpasswd)` returns `[status, user]`: `[200, user]` when
the credentials are right, otherwise `[401, ""]`.

- `header` is the value of the `Authorization` request header, or `None`/empty when absent. A valid one looks like
  `Basic dXNlcjpwYXNz`: the word `Basic`, one space, then the **Base64** encoding of `user:password` (UTF-8). The
  password may itself contain colons; the user name ends at the **first** colon.
- `htpasswd` is a list of lines `user:stored`. The **first** line for the user decides. Two storage schemes are
  supported:
  - `{PLAIN}secret`: the password in clear text;
  - `{SHA}xxxx`: Base64 of the SHA-1 digest of the password.
  Any other scheme cannot be verified and means 401.

Return 401 for: a missing header, a scheme other than `Basic`, text that is not valid Base64 or not valid UTF-8, no
colon in the decoded text, an unknown user, or a wrong password. User names and passwords are case-sensitive.

**Example:** header for `rosa` / `tea-time`, file `["rosa:{SHA}...digest of tea-time..."]` → `[200, "rosa"]`
nginx-basic-auth.starter:
import base64, hashlib

def basic_auth(header, htpasswd):
    # return [200, user] or [401, ""]
    pass

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *HTTP basic authentication and auth subrequests*. The `base64` and `hashlib` modules.
guide.intuition: Basic authentication is two encodings and a comparison. The browser packs `user:password` in Base64, which is a packaging format and not encryption. The server unpacks it, finds the user's line, transforms the offered password the same way the stored one was transformed, and compares.
hints: Reject early: no header, wrong scheme, undecodable text, no colon.
Split on the first colon only: `decoded.split(":", 1)`.
For `{SHA}`, hash the offered password with SHA-1, Base64-encode the raw digest, and compare strings.
guide.brute_force: There is no meaningful slower variant; the file is scanned once. What matters is the order of the refusals and never raising an exception on hostile input.
guide.approach:
1. Validate the header and decode inside `try`.
2. Split into user and password.
3. Find the first line whose name equals the user.
4. Verify according to the scheme prefix; unknown scheme fails.

Dry run: header `Basic c2FtOnBhOnNzOndvcmQ=` decodes to `sam:pa:ss:word`. First colon → user `sam`, password `pa:ss:word`. The line `sam:{PLAIN}pa:ss:word` matches → `[200, "sam"]`.
guide.complexity: Time O(number of htpasswd lines); space O(1).
guide.pitfalls: Splitting at the last colon; comparing names without regard to case; accepting when a later duplicate line matches; letting bad Base64 raise an exception; believing Base64 protects the password (it does not; TLS does).
guide.follow_up: SHA-1 without a salt is weak. Add the salted `{SSHA}` scheme: Base64 of the SHA-1 of password plus salt, followed by the salt.

nginx-jwt-check.title: Validate a JSON Web Token (HS256)
nginx-jwt-check.description:
Write the validation a gateway performs on a JSON Web Token signed with HMAC-SHA256.

`jwt_check(token, secret, now, issuer, audience)` returns `[status, reason]`. A token is three **Base64URL** parts
joined by dots: `header.payload.signature`. Base64URL uses `-` and `_` and omits the `=` padding, so add padding back
before decoding. The header and payload are JSON objects.

Check in this order and stop at the first failure:

1. Not exactly three parts, or a part that cannot be decoded, or header/payload that are not JSON objects
   → `[401, "malformed"]`.
2. Header `alg` is not `"HS256"` → `[401, "algorithm not accepted"]`.
3. The signature is not the HMAC-SHA256 of the text `header.payload` (the two encoded parts with the dot, as received)
   under `secret` → `[401, "bad signature"]`.
4. Claim `exp` is missing or `exp <= now` → `[401, "expired"]`.
5. Claim `nbf` is present and `nbf > now` → `[401, "not yet valid"]`.
6. Claim `iss` differs from `issuer`, or `aud` differs from `audience` → `[401, "wrong issuer or audience"]`.

Otherwise return `[200, "ok"]`. `secret` is a string; use its UTF-8 bytes as the key.
nginx-jwt-check.starter:
import base64, hashlib, hmac, json

def jwt_check(token, secret, now, issuer, audience):
    # return [200, "ok"] or [401, reason]
    pass

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *JSON Web Tokens and OpenID Connect*. The `base64`, `hmac`, `hashlib` and `json` modules.
guide.intuition: A token is a signed note. Nothing written in it may be believed until the signature has been checked, because anyone can write a note. So the order is fixed: can it be parsed, is the algorithm the one we use, is the signature ours, and only then what do the claims say.
hints: Restore padding with `part + "=" * (-len(part) % 4)` before `urlsafe_b64decode`.
Sign exactly the first two parts as they arrived, joined by a dot. Do not re-encode the JSON.
Compare signatures with `hmac.compare_digest`, and treat a missing `exp` as expired.
guide.brute_force: Checking the claims first and the signature last gives the same accept/reject decision for honest tokens but reports the wrong reason for forged ones and, worse, tempts code into trusting unverified claims. Keep the signature check ahead of every claim.
guide.approach:
1. Split into three; decode each inside `try`.
2. Require `alg == HS256`. This also defeats the classic `alg: none` attack.
3. Recompute the HMAC over `parts[0] + "." + parts[1]` and compare.
4. `exp`, then `nbf`, then `iss` and `aud`.

Dry run for the forged token: header and payload decode fine and `alg` is HS256. The attacker changed `sub` to `admin`, so the bytes that were signed differ and the recomputed HMAC does not equal the old signature → `bad signature`.
guide.complexity: Time O(length of the token); space O(length of the token).
guide.pitfalls: Accepting `alg: none`; verifying after reading claims; forgetting Base64URL padding; `exp < now` instead of `<=`; accepting a token with no `exp`; comparing with `==` (timing leak).
guide.follow_up: Support RS256: verification with a public key chosen by the header's `kid` from a key set, which is how tokens from an identity provider are checked.

nginx-access-control.title: allow, deny and satisfy
nginx-access-control.description:
Combine NGINX's address rules with authentication. `access_check(rules, client_ip, satisfy, auth_ok)` returns the
status code: `200`, `401` or `403`.

**Address rules.** `rules` is a list of `[action, target]` in order, where `action` is `"allow"` or `"deny"` and
`target` is `"all"`, an IPv4 address (`"203.0.113.5"`) or a network in CIDR form (`"10.0.0.0/8"`). The **first** rule
whose target contains the client address decides. The outcome is one of: *allowed*, *denied*, or *no rule matched*.

**Authentication.** `auth_ok` is `None` when no authentication is configured, otherwise `True` or `False` for whether
the client presented valid credentials.

**Combining them:**

- No authentication configured: denied → `403`, otherwise `200`.
- `satisfy` is `"all"` (the default): denied → `403`; otherwise credentials must be valid: `200` or `401`.
- `satisfy` is `"any"`: allowed by a matching `allow` rule → `200`; otherwise valid credentials → `200`; otherwise
  `401`. ("No rule matched" does not grant access here.)

A network `a.b.c.d/n` contains an address when their first `n` bits are equal. `/0` contains everything.

**Example:** `[["allow", "10.0.0.0/8"], ["deny", "all"]]`, `"10.2.3.4"`, `"all"`, `None` → `200`;
with `"203.0.113.9"` → `403`

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *Access rules, satisfy, CORS and secure links*. Bit operations, or the `ipaddress` module.
guide.intuition: The address rules work like a list of bouncers in a queue: the first one who recognises you decides, and the rest are never asked. `satisfy` then says whether the address check and the password check are both required (`all`) or whether either is enough (`any`).
hints: Convert an address to one 32-bit integer; then "same network" is a comparison after masking.
The mask for `/n` has n one-bits at the top: `((1 << n) - 1) << (32 - n)`.
Keep three outcomes for the address check, not two. Under `satisfy any` only an explicit allow grants access.
guide.brute_force: Compare addresses as strings with `startswith`. It works for `/8`, `/16` and `/24` written on octet boundaries and fails for every other prefix length, such as `/12` or `/25`.
guide.approach:
1. Parse the client address to an integer.
2. Walk the rules; on the first hit remember the action and stop.
3. Branch on `auth_ok is None`, then on `satisfy`.

Dry run: rules `allow 192.168.0.0/16; deny all;`, client `8.8.8.8`, `satisfy any`, valid credentials. The first rule does not contain the address; `deny all` does → denied. Under `any`, the address did not grant access, but the credentials do → 200. With `satisfy all` the same request is 403.
guide.complexity: Time O(number of rules); space O(1).
guide.pitfalls: Letting the last matching rule win; string-prefix matching of networks; returning 403 instead of 401 when credentials would have been enough; treating "no rule matched" as an allow under `satisfy any`; a shift by 32 for `/0`.
guide.follow_up: Support IPv6 targets and the `geo` block's "most specific network wins" rule, which differs from first match.

nginx-cors-preflight.title: CORS: Preflight and Response Headers
nginx-cors-preflight.description:
Browsers ask permission before letting a page on one origin call an API on another. Implement the decision a typical
NGINX CORS configuration makes.

`cors(method, origin, acr_method, allowed_origins, allowed_methods)` returns `[status, headers]`:

- `method`: the request method.
- `origin`: the `Origin` request header, or `""` if absent.
- `acr_method`: the `Access-Control-Request-Method` request header, or `""`.
- `allowed_origins`: the exact origins that may call the API.
- `allowed_methods`: the methods to advertise.

`status` is `204` when NGINX answers the request itself and `0` when the request is passed to the application.
`headers` is a dictionary of response headers NGINX adds.

Rules:

1. No `Origin` header → `[0, {}]`. It is not a cross-origin request.
2. A **preflight** is a request with method `OPTIONS` **and** a non-empty `acr_method`. Preflights are answered with
   status `204`; everything else has status `0`.
3. Whenever `Origin` is present, add `"Vary": "Origin"`.
4. If the origin is in `allowed_origins` (exact, case-sensitive comparison), add
   `"Access-Control-Allow-Origin": origin`. For a preflight also add
   `"Access-Control-Allow-Methods"`: the allowed methods joined with `", "`, and `"Access-Control-Max-Age": "86400"`.
5. If the origin is not allowed, add nothing more. The browser will block the call.

**Example:** `"OPTIONS"`, `"https://app.shop.test"`, `"POST"`, `["https://app.shop.test"]`, `["GET", "POST"]` →
`[204, {"Vary": "Origin", "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "https://app.shop.test", "Access-Control-Allow-Methods": "GET, POST", "Access-Control-Max-Age": "86400"}]`

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *Access rules, satisfy, CORS and secure links*. Dictionaries.
guide.intuition: CORS is enforced by the browser, not the server. The server's whole job is to state, in response headers, which origins it trusts. A preflight is the browser asking in advance; the reply needs no body, only the permission headers. A server that echoes back any origin has switched the protection off.
hints: Start with the non-CORS case: no `Origin`, no headers, pass through.
Compute `preflight` once and use it for both the status and the extra headers.
Compare the origin with `in allowed_origins`. Prefix or suffix matching lets look-alike domains through.
guide.brute_force: Not applicable; the function is constant time. The naive version returns `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` with whatever origin was sent, which makes every site on the internet an allowed caller.
guide.approach:
1. Empty origin → `[0, {}]`.
2. `preflight = method == OPTIONS and acr_method`.
3. `headers = {Vary: Origin}`.
4. Allowed → add the origin; if preflight add methods and max age.
5. Status 204 for preflight, else 0.

Dry run: `OPTIONS` from `https://evil.example` asking for `DELETE`. It is a preflight, so status 204. The origin is not allowed, so only `Vary: Origin` is returned and the browser refuses to send the real request.
guide.complexity: Time O(number of allowed origins); space O(1).
guide.pitfalls: Reflecting any origin; `startswith` matching, fooled by `https://app.shop.test.evil.example`; ignoring scheme or case differences, which make a different origin; treating every `OPTIONS` as a preflight; omitting `Vary: Origin`, which lets a shared cache serve one origin's permission to another.
guide.follow_up: Add credentialed requests: `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, which browsers accept only with an explicit origin, never with `*`, and `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` echoing the requested headers from an allow-list.

nginx-https-hsts.title: HTTPS Redirects, the Canonical Host and HSTS
nginx-https-hsts.description:
A site must be reachable only as `https://CANONICAL`. Decide what NGINX answers.

`https_redirect(scheme, host, uri, forwarded_proto, canonical, hsts_max_age)` returns `[status, location, hsts]`:

- `scheme`: `"http"` or `"https"`, as NGINX itself sees the connection.
- `host`: the `Host` header; it may be in any letter case and may carry a `:port`.
- `uri`: the request URI including any query string.
- `forwarded_proto`: the `X-Forwarded-Proto` header set by a trusted load balancer that terminates TLS, or `""` when
  there is no such balancer. When non-empty it **replaces** `scheme` as the scheme the client used.
- `canonical`: the one allowed host name, lower-case, without a port.
- `hsts_max_age`: seconds for the `Strict-Transport-Security` header; `0` means the header is not used.

Rules:

1. If the client's scheme is not `https`: `[301, "https://" + canonical + uri, ""]`. HSTS is never sent over plain
   HTTP.
2. Otherwise, if the host (lower-cased, port removed) is not the canonical one:
   `[301, "https://" + canonical + uri, hsts]`.
3. Otherwise `[200, "", hsts]`.

`hsts` is `"max-age=N"` when `hsts_max_age > 0`, else `""`.

**Example:** `"http"`, `"www.shop.test"`, `"/tea?x=1"`, `""`, `"shop.test"`, `300`
→ `[301, "https://shop.test/tea?x=1", ""]`

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *TLS, HTTPS redirects, HSTS and upstream encryption*. Basic string handling.
guide.intuition: There are four ways to type the address and only one is wanted. Every other form gets a single permanent redirect straight to the wanted one. The only subtlety is knowing which scheme the *client* used when a balancer in front has already removed the encryption.
hints: Work out the client's scheme first: the forwarded header when present, otherwise NGINX's own.
Normalise the host before comparing: lower-case, port removed.
Redirect directly to the canonical HTTPS URL in both cases, so nobody needs two hops.
guide.brute_force: Redirect in two steps, first to HTTPS on the same host and then to the canonical host. It ends in the right place but costs an extra round trip, and needs a certificate for every alias.
guide.approach:
1. `client_scheme = forwarded_proto or scheme`.
2. `name = host.lower().split(':')[0]`.
3. Build the HSTS string.
4. Not HTTPS → 301 without HSTS. Wrong host → 301 with HSTS. Else 200 with HSTS.

Dry run: NGINX sees `http` (the balancer forwards plain HTTP) and `X-Forwarded-Proto: https`, host `shop.test`. The client's scheme is `https` and the host is canonical → `[200, "", "max-age=300"]`. Had the header been ignored, the answer would be a redirect to the URL the client is already on, repeated for ever.
guide.complexity: Time and space O(length of the URL).
guide.pitfalls: Ignoring `X-Forwarded-Proto` behind a TLS-terminating balancer, which causes a redirect loop; sending HSTS over HTTP, where browsers ignore it; redirecting to the same host over HTTPS first; dropping the query string; comparing hosts case-sensitively.
guide.follow_up: Add `includeSubDomains` and `preload` options to the HSTS value, and refuse `preload` unless `max-age` is at least one year, as the preload list requires.

nginx-log-parse.title: Parse an Access Log Line
nginx-log-parse.description:
Turn one line of NGINX's default `combined` access log into a dictionary. The format is

```
$remote_addr - $remote_user [$time_local] "$request" $status $body_bytes_sent "$http_referer" "$http_user_agent"
```

`parse_log(line)` returns a dictionary with these keys, or `None` if the line does not have this shape:

| Key | Value |
|---|---|
| `addr`, `user`, `time`, `referer`, `agent` | the text of the field, unchanged (`-` stays `-`) |
| `status`, `bytes` | integers |
| `method`, `uri`, `protocol` | the three space-separated parts of the request |

Details:

- Ignore whitespace at the ends of the line. The line must contain exactly these fields and nothing after them.
- The address and user contain no spaces. The time is whatever stands between `[` and `]`. The status is exactly
  three digits. Quoted fields contain no `"` (NGINX writes a quote inside a value as `\x22`).
- Scanners send requests that are not HTTP. If the quoted request does not consist of exactly three parts separated
  by single spaces, set `method` and `protocol` to `""` and `uri` to the whole request text.

**Example:** `203.0.113.9 - rosa [21/Nov/2026:14:02:11 +0800] "GET /a?b=1 HTTP/1.1" 200 512 "-" "curl/8.5.0"`
→ `{"addr": "203.0.113.9", "user": "rosa", "time": "21/Nov/2026:14:02:11 +0800", "method": "GET", "uri": "/a?b=1", "protocol": "HTTP/1.1", "status": 200, "bytes": 512, "referer": "-", "agent": "curl/8.5.0"}`
nginx-log-parse.starter:
import re

def parse_log(line):
    # return a dictionary of fields, or None
    pass

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *Access logs, error logs and request tracing*. Regular expressions with groups.
guide.intuition: The line is a sentence with fixed punctuation: a hyphen, square brackets around the time, quotes around three free-text fields. Describe that punctuation in one regular expression and let it cut the fields out. Splitting on spaces cannot work, because the time and the user agent contain spaces.
hints: Anchor the pattern at both ends with `^` and `$` so that lines with extra fields are rejected.
Capture the whole quoted request first, then split it yourself. That keeps malformed requests from making the whole line fail.
Use `[^"]*` for quoted fields and `[^\]]+` for the time.
guide.brute_force: `line.split(" ")` and pick fields by position. It breaks on the first user agent containing a space, and on any request that is not three words.
guide.approach:
1. Compile one pattern with eight groups.
2. `match` against the stripped line; no match → `None`.
3. Split the request on single spaces; exactly three non-empty parts → method, URI, protocol; otherwise keep it whole as the URI.
4. Convert status and bytes to integers and build the dictionary.

Dry run on the scanner line with request `\x16\x03\x01`: the overall pattern matches, the request has one part, so `method=""`, `uri="\x16\x03\x01"`, `protocol=""`, status 400.
guide.complexity: Time O(length of the line); space O(length of the line).
guide.pitfalls: Splitting on spaces; returning `None` for malformed requests, which hides attack traffic from the statistics; accepting lines from a different log format; forgetting IPv6 addresses contain colons, not dots.
guide.follow_up: Parse a custom format with `rt=$request_time urt=$upstream_response_time`, where the upstream time may be `-` or a comma-separated list after retries.

args: 2001:db8::7 - - [21/Nov/2026:14:02:13 +0800] "POST /api/login HTTP/2.0" 429 0 "https://shop.test/login" "Mozilla/5.0 (iPhone; CPU iPhone OS 18_0 like Mac OS X)"

expected.agent: Mozilla/5.0 (iPhone; CPU iPhone OS 18_0 like Mac OS X)

args: not a log line at all

nginx-log-topn.title: Summarise an Access Log: Top Clients, Error Rate, p95
nginx-log-topn.description:
Given parsed access-log entries, compute the three numbers an on-call engineer asks for first.

`log_summary(entries, n)` receives `entries`, a list of `[address, status, request_time]`, and returns
`[top, error_rate, p95]`:

- `top`: the `n` addresses with the most requests, as `[address, count]` pairs, highest count first. Break ties by
  address in ascending string order. If there are fewer than `n` distinct addresses, return them all.
- `error_rate`: the fraction of entries with a status from 500 to 599, rounded to 4 decimal places.
- `p95`: the 95th percentile of `request_time` by the **nearest-rank** method: sort the times in ascending order and
  take the value at position `ceil(0.95 * count)`, counting from 1.

For an empty list return `[[], 0.0, 0.0]`.

**Example:** `[["a", 200, 0.1], ["b", 502, 2.0], ["a", 200, 0.3], ["a", 404, 0.2]]`, `n=1`
→ `[[["a", 3]], 0.25, 2.0]`

guide.prereqs: Lessons: *Access logs, error logs and request tracing* and *Workers, connections, keepalive and OS tuning* (percentiles). Sorting with a key.
guide.intuition: Three classic aggregations over one list: a frequency count, a ratio, and an order statistic. Each answers a different question: who is hitting us, how much is failing, and how slow is the slow tail.
hints: Count with a dictionary, then sort the items by `(-count, address)` to get both orderings in one key.
Only 5xx counts as a server error here. 4xx and NGINX's 499 are the client's doing.
Nearest rank needs a ceiling. With integers, `-(-95 * n // 100)` is `ceil(0.95 * n)` without floating point.
guide.brute_force: For the top list, repeatedly scan for the most frequent remaining address: O(n × distinct). Sorting the counts once is O(d log d).
guide.approach:
1. Empty input → the fixed answer.
2. Count addresses; sort; cut to `n`.
3. Count statuses in 500..599; divide; round.
4. Sort the times; rank = ceil(0.95 × count); take index `rank - 1`.

Dry run of the example: counts a=3, b=1 → top 1 is `[a, 3]`. One 5xx out of four → 0.25. Sorted times 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 2.0; rank = ceil(3.8) = 4 → 2.0.
guide.complexity: Time O(n log n) for the two sorts; space O(n).
guide.pitfalls: An off-by-one in the percentile (indexing with `int(0.95 * n)` picks the next element); leaving tie order to chance; counting 4xx as errors; dividing by zero on an empty log; float rounding in `0.95 * n` for sizes such as 20.
guide.follow_up: Process a log too large for memory: keep the counts in a dictionary but estimate the percentile from a fixed-size histogram of buckets.

nginx-status-diagnosis.title: 502, 504 or 499? Follow the Upstream Attempts
nginx-status-diagnosis.description:
Work out the status code a proxied request ends with, and after how many seconds, when NGINX tries upstream servers
one after another.

`upstream_outcome(attempts, connect_timeout, read_timeout, client_patience)`:

- `attempts` lists, in the order NGINX tries them, what each server does:
  - `["refused"]`: the connection is refused at once. Takes 0 seconds. An error.
  - `["closed"]`: the server accepts and immediately closes without answering. 0 seconds. An error.
  - `["connect_hang"]`: no reply to the connection attempt. NGINX gives up after `connect_timeout` seconds. A timeout.
  - `["respond", s]`: the server connects at once and sends its response after `s` seconds. If `s > read_timeout`,
    NGINX gives up after `read_timeout` seconds: a timeout. Otherwise the request succeeds after `s` seconds.
- After an error or timeout NGINX moves to the next attempt, and the time spent adds up.
- A success ends with status `200`.
- If every attempt fails, the status comes from the **last** failure: `502` for an error, `504` for a timeout.
- An empty list means no server was available: `502` after 0 seconds.
- The client waits `client_patience` seconds in total. If the moment of the final outcome, successful or not, is
  **later** than that, the result is `[499, client_patience]`: the client closed the connection first.

Return `[status, seconds]`.

**Example:** `[["refused"], ["respond", 2]]`, `5`, `60`, `120` → `[200, 2]`

**Example:** `[["connect_hang"], ["respond", 90]]`, `5`, `60`, `120` → `[504, 65]`

guide.prereqs: Lesson: *A troubleshooting method and the gateway status codes*. Loops and conditionals.
